title: HE PUT A RING ON HER FINGER. THAT DID NOT GIVE HIM THE RIGHT TO VIOLATE HER BODY.
paragraphs: HE PUT A RING ON HER FINGER. THAT DID NOT GIVE HIM THE RIGHT TO VIOLATE HER BODY.
Can a Husband Commit Sexual Violence Against His Own Wife? What the Church Must Never Excuse — And Why the Gospel Demands That We Stop Confusing Marriage With Ownership.
She was lying beside the man she had promised to love for the rest of her life.
The same man who stood before God, held her hands, and vowed to cherish her.
The same man who once told her she was safe with him.
But that night, she was afraid.
She had already said no.
Maybe she was exhausted. Maybe she was hurting. Maybe something inside her was simply not ready.
She tried to explain.
He didn't want to hear it.
And somewhere between her whispered refusal and his insistence that she was his wife, something happened that she would struggle to put into words for years.
Not because she didn't know what happened.
But because she had been taught that a good Christian wife should never refuse her husband.
She remembered the sermons about submission.
She remembered the warnings about denying a husband's needs.
She remembered hearing that her body belonged to him.
But she couldn't remember anyone telling her what to do when the person who promised to protect her became the person she feared.
So she remained silent.
And the following Sunday, she sat beside him in church.
He sang.
She stared at the floor.
He raised his hands in worship.
She tried not to cry.
And nobody knew.
Nobody knew that the woman sitting quietly in the pew was carrying a question she was terrified to ask.
Can my own husband sexually violate me, even though we're married?
The answer is yes.
And if that answer makes us uncomfortable, perhaps we need to ask why the suffering of a wife has become less disturbing to us than the possibility of confronting a husband.
Because there are wounds the Church must never cover with religious language.
There are sins we must never rename as marital rights.
And there are women who have spent years believing that honoring God means surrendering their right to bodily safety.
It is time to open the Scriptures carefully.
Not to make the Bible say what our culture wants.
Not to erase the beauty of marriage.
But to confront what happens when God's Word is twisted into permission to harm someone He created in His image.
And before we go any further, remember this:
A wedding vow is not permission for sexual violence. A marriage covenant does not cancel a person's humanity. And a husband's desire does not turn his wife's refusal into sin.
The Bible begins its understanding of marriage long before it speaks about marital responsibilities.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים (be-tselem Elohim) means "in the image of God."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say the man bears God's image while the woman merely exists to satisfy him.
Both are created in God's image.
Both possess dignity that marriage does not erase.
Both are morally accountable before the Lord.
When Genesis 2:24 describes the man and woman becoming בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad), "one flesh," it reveals the profound union of marriage.
But becoming one flesh does not mean one person ceases to be a person.
Unity is not ownership.
Intimacy is not domination.
And covenant faithfulness is not permission to disregard another person's fear, pain, or refusal.
Somebody needs to hear that, especially the woman who has been told that because she said yes at the altar, she lost the right to say no in the bedroom.
You did not stop being made in God's image when you became someone's wife.
And no human being acquires unlimited authority over another person's body through marriage.
But what about 1 Corinthians 7?
This is where the conversation becomes difficult.
And this is where we must refuse to become careless with Scripture.
The apostle Paul writes:
Some have taken the first half of that verse and used it like a weapon.
They quote the wife's obligation.
Then they conveniently forget the husband's.
They emphasize authority.
Then they ignore reciprocity.
They speak of marital intimacy as though the husband possesses a divine entitlement to sexual access, regardless of his wife's condition or willingness.
But read the entire verse.
Paul deliberately speaks in both directions.
The Greek expression ἐξουσιάζει (exousiazei) conveys exercising authority or having authority over.
And the same verb is applied to both spouses.
Paul's instruction challenges unilateral control rather than establishing it.
The surrounding passage, 1 Corinthians 7:3–5, teaches mutual marital responsibility, consideration, and agreement. Verse 5 specifically recognizes mutual consent regarding periods of abstinence.
This passage affirms that sexual intimacy matters within marriage.
It does not authorize rape.
It does not instruct a husband to ignore his wife's resistance.
It does not grant permission to use intimidation, threats, restraint, or physical force.
And it certainly does not suggest that one spouse may commit violence to enforce what they believe the other owes them.
The text addresses marital obligations within a relationship of mutual responsibility. It is not a procedure for compelling sexual activity.
A spouse can neglect marital intimacy in ways that deserve honest conversation, counseling, and spiritual care.
But neglect, disagreement, or refusal never gives the other spouse permission to commit sexual violence.
A marital responsibility is not a license to force its fulfillment.
Imagine how differently some marriages might look if we taught the entire passage instead of using half a verse to silence half the marriage.
And then consider Ephesians 5.
The passage many people associate with wives submitting to husbands also gives husbands a command that should make every abusive man tremble at the seriousness of his responsibility.
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (Ephesians 5:25, KJV)
The Greek word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) is the command to love.
But Paul does not leave the meaning of that love to the husband's imagination.
He gives its pattern.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who gave Himself.
The Lord who served.
The Bridegroom whose love was sacrificial rather than exploitative.
Think about that.
Christ did not demonstrate His love by exploiting the vulnerability of His people.
He laid down His life for them.
And a husband who claims Christ as his model cannot justify treating his wife's vulnerability as an opportunity to overpower her.
Ephesians 5:28–29 continues by calling husbands to love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them.
The Greek word ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei) conveys nourishing or caring for.
Θάλπει (thalpei) carries the sense of cherishing or tenderly caring for.
These are not words describing cruelty.
They describe care.
A man cannot credibly claim to cherish his wife's body while deliberately using it against her will.
He cannot invoke Christlike love while making her afraid of what happens when he is displeased.
And he cannot transform sexual violence into righteousness simply by attaching the word "marriage" to it.
Colossians 3:19 makes the command unmistakable:
"Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." (KJV)
The Greek μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikrainesthe) prohibits becoming bitter or harsh toward them.
The precise context concerns marital conduct, not a modern legal definition of sexual assault. But the moral direction is clear: Christian husbands are commanded toward love, not cruelty.
If harshness is forbidden, how could sexual brutality be defended as holy?
If husbands are commanded to cherish, how could deliberate violation be excused as obedience?
And if Jesus is our model, why would we defend conduct that contradicts His character?
There is another passage that deserves attention.
First Peter 3:7 instructs husbands to dwell with their wives according to knowledge, giving honor to them as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
The Greek word τιμή (timē) refers to honor or value.
Not possession.
Honor.
The passage even warns husbands that their prayers may be hindered when they fail in their responsibilities.
Think about the seriousness of that warning.
A man can appear religious.
He can attend church.
He can speak eloquently about Scripture.
He can lead prayers in public.
But his treatment of his wife still matters before God.
His private behavior is not hidden from the Lord simply because the congregation admires his public ministry.
And this is where the Church must confront something painful.
Sometimes the person asking for help is told to pray harder, submit more, become more affectionate, dress differently, or stop provoking her husband.
Sometimes a woman discloses sexual coercion and receives a lecture about her marital duties instead of concern for her safety.
Sometimes church leaders fear the scandal of exposing abuse more than the injustice of allowing it to continue.
Sometimes the language of forgiveness becomes a demand for silence.
And sometimes the very community that should help carry the wounded toward Christ becomes another place where they are afraid to speak.
That must never become normal.
A church does not protect the sanctity of marriage by protecting sexual violence.
It does not honor the Gospel by pressuring victims to remain silent.
And it does not preserve Christian testimony by hiding wrongdoing behind the reputation of a respected husband, ministry leader, or family.
A church that protects an abuser's reputation at the expense of a victim's safety has confused institutional image with biblical righteousness.
Consider what the prophet Isaiah declared:
"Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow." (Isaiah 1:17, KJV)
The Hebrew command דִּרְשׁוּ מִשְׁפָּט (dirshu mishpat) means "seek justice."
The call to justice is not an optional decoration of biblical faith.
It is part of God's demand that His people practice righteousness.
Psalm 82:3–4 likewise commands the defense of the vulnerable and their deliverance from the hand of the wicked.
These passages do not specifically address marital sexual assault. Their broader moral principles, however, forbid treating the vulnerable as disposable.
The Church must apply those principles faithfully.
We must also remember the difference between forgiveness and the removal of consequences.
Forgiveness is central to the Gospel.
But forgiveness is not a command to pretend that evil never happened.
Repentance does not mean avoiding accountability.
Reconciliation is not the same as forgiveness, and reconciliation cannot be demanded where safety, truth, and genuine change are absent.
A woman can pursue healing in Christ without immediately trusting someone who harmed her.
She can seek protection without betraying her faith.
She can report a crime without rejecting the Gospel.
She can establish boundaries without becoming an enemy of marriage.
And she should never be pressured to prove her forgiveness by accepting further sexual access or returning to danger.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining and addressing wrongdoing.
The Church must not act as though spiritual counseling replaces the responsibility of civil authorities where crimes may have occurred.
Laws differ by jurisdiction, but marriage does not automatically remove criminal responsibility for sexual assault. The specific legal definitions and remedies depend on the applicable law.
The Church must never promise confidentiality in ways that obstruct legally required reporting or prevent appropriate protection.
Pastoral care should be compassionate, trauma-informed, and attentive to safety.
Where coercion or violence is alleged, couples counseling should not be imposed as the first solution, because it can expose the harmed spouse to further intimidation or retaliation.
Safety comes first.
Truth matters.
Accountability matters.
And so does the spiritual condition of the person who committed the harm.
Because the Gospel is not only a message of comfort to the wounded.
It is also a summons to repentance for the one who wounds.
To the husband who has used threats, pressure, fear, physical force, or religious language to obtain sexual access from his wife:
Do not hide behind your wedding vows.
Do not quote 1 Corinthians 7 while ignoring Ephesians 5.
Do not confuse your sexual desire with divine authority.
And do not assume that because your wife stopped resisting, she freely agreed.
Fear can silence a person.
Exhaustion can silence a person.
The knowledge that resistance will lead to punishment can silence a person.
Silence is not necessarily consent.
A marriage certificate is not consent.
Previous sexual intimacy is not consent to every future encounter.
And compliance under threats or force is not freely given agreement.
You may have convinced yourself that you were exercising a husband's rights.
But if you used coercion or violence, you must face the seriousness of what you did.
Stop the harmful behavior.
Respect your wife's boundaries and safety.
Do not pressure her to forgive, reconcile, withdraw a report, or conceal what happened.
Seek appropriate professional help and submit to lawful accountability.
And repent.
Not merely because you fear exposure.
Not because you want to save your reputation.
Not because you want your wife to return to the way things were.
Repent because sin is an offense against the God who made her.
Second Corinthians 7:10–11 describes godly sorrow as producing repentance and earnestness.
Real repentance is more than tears after being confronted.
It is a turning away from evil.
It does not demand instant trust as payment for an apology.
It does not blame the victim for the offender's actions.
And it does not treat consequences as persecution.
God's grace is real.
Forgiveness through Jesus Christ is real.
But grace must never be twisted into permission to continue harming another person.
The cross is not a hiding place for unrepentant cruelty.
It is where the seriousness of sin and the mercy of God meet.
And to the wife who recognizes herself somewhere in these words:
Perhaps you have been carrying a kind of shame you cannot explain.
Perhaps you have wondered whether you were selfish.
Perhaps someone told you that refusing sex made you a disobedient Christian wife.
Perhaps you have learned to avoid conflict by giving in, even when you feel frightened or distressed.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that the pain you experienced was simply part of marriage.
Please hear this carefully.
What someone did to you is not made righteous because that person is your spouse.
You are not required to call violence love.
You are not required to call coercion submission.
You are not required to call fear peace.
And you are not required to sacrifice your safety to preserve someone else's appearance of godliness.
Jesus knows what it means to be betrayed.
He knows what it means to suffer injustice.
He knows what it means for powerful people to misuse their authority.
And He does not ask us to pretend evil is good.
In Luke 4:18, Jesus announces good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed, drawing from Isaiah's prophetic language.
This does not mean every painful circumstance will immediately disappear.
Nor does it mean a particular marriage will necessarily be restored.
It means the mission of Christ cannot honestly be used to celebrate oppression.
The Gospel announces redemption, truth, mercy, and the coming reign of God's righteousness.
Jesus is not indifferent to the wounded.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (KJV)
You may not feel close to God right now.
You may struggle to pray.
You may be angry that people who spoke in His name failed to protect you.
You may even find it difficult to enter a church building.
Your pain deserves to be taken seriously.
You do not have to perform spiritual strength to receive compassionate help.

If you are currently unsafe, prioritize getting to a safer place when possible and contacting emergency services, a trusted person, a qualified domestic-violence service, or appropriate local authorities. If your communications are monitored, seek help through a safer device or trusted contact when you can.
You do not need to wait for a church committee to decide whether your suffering is serious enough to deserve protection.
And if you are a pastor, elder, counselor, ministry leader, or Christian friend reading this, there is a question you must confront.
What happens when a woman trusts you enough to tell you what happened?
Will you listen?
Will you believe that her disclosure deserves a serious, compassionate response without assuming you already know every fact?
Will you resist the temptation to protect the reputation of someone influential?
Will you avoid turning the first conversation into a debate about submission?
Will you help her access qualified support and appropriate reporting channels?
Will you remember that safeguarding a vulnerable person is not an attack on biblical marriage?
Or will you send her back into danger with a Bible verse she has already heard used against her?
James 1:27 speaks of pure religion as caring for vulnerable people in their affliction and keeping oneself unspotted from the world.
That is a demanding picture of faith.
Not merely preaching compassion.
Practicing it.
Not merely defending marriage as an institution.
Protecting the people within it.
Not merely condemning sexual sin outside marriage.
Having the courage to confront sexual violence inside marriage.
Because sexual violence does not become less serious when the perpetrator wears a wedding ring.
And the suffering of a wife does not become less important when the person responsible is her husband.
This is not a rejection of Christian marriage.
It is a defense of what marriage was meant to be.
A covenant marked by faithfulness.
A relationship in which love seeks the other's good.
A union in which intimacy is not obtained through terror.
A home where strength is used to protect rather than dominate.
A marriage where both husband and wife can speak honestly without fearing retaliation.
A place where the teaching of Christ is not merely displayed on the wall but reflected in the way two people treat each other when nobody else is watching.
And perhaps that is the question we have avoided for too long.
What does a Christian home actually look like when the church doors are closed?
When there is no pastor watching?
When there is no congregation to impress?
When a wife says, "I'm not comfortable"?
When she is tired?
When she is sick?
When she is afraid?
Does her husband remember that she is his fellow image-bearer, worthy of tenderness and honor?
Or does he believe that his vows entitle him to take what she has not freely agreed to give?
The answer reveals something important about his understanding of love.
Because the Gospel never teaches that power makes a person righteous.
Jesus taught His followers that greatness is expressed through service, not domination (Mark 10:42–45).
And the husband who wants to lead like Christ must first learn to love like Christ.
Not selectively.
Not only in public.
Not only when his wife agrees.
But especially when his desires and her well-being seem to come into conflict.
That is where character is revealed.
And that is where the Church must stop excusing what Scripture never commanded.
There may be someone reading this who has never told another person what happened.
Someone who has carried the secret for ten years.
Someone who still sleeps beside the person who hurt her.
Someone who has left but continues to struggle with guilt.
Someone who fears that telling the truth will destroy the family.
Someone who wonders whether God will be disappointed if she seeks protection.
I cannot promise that speaking will be easy.
I cannot promise that every church leader will respond wisely.
I cannot promise that the people you love will understand immediately.
But I can tell you this:
God's Word does not require you to rename sexual violence as marital obedience.
And seeking safety does not mean you have abandoned Jesus.
There is hope beyond what happened to you.
Healing may take time.
It may involve trusted friends, skilled counselors, medical care, legal protection, and the difficult work of rebuilding a sense of safety.
Your journey may not look like anyone else's.
And you do not owe the public your story.
But what happened does not have to become the final definition of your life.
That is why we keep returning to the Gospel.
Because the Gospel is not the promise that every earthly relationship will be repaired.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ entered our broken world, bore sin, conquered death, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
His resurrection declares that evil and death do not have the final word.
And His coming kingdom promises a justice no human institution can perfectly provide.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise does not excuse delaying justice today.
It gives us reason to pursue righteousness while waiting for the fullness of God's restoration.
This is what we mean at Gospel Warrior when we speak about the journey from scandal to grace.
Not hiding the scandal.
Not minimizing the wound.
Not forcing a victim to reconcile.
Not offering an offender cheap absolution.
But bringing what is hidden into the light of God's truth.
Calling sin what it is.
Calling the guilty to genuine repentance.
Standing beside those who have been harmed.
And pointing every broken heart toward the Savior who alone can ultimately redeem what sin has devastated.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by offering a future that is not finally ruled by it.
If this article has opened your eyes to something the Church needs to confront, please don't let the conversation end here.
Someone may finally realize that marriage does not erase their dignity.
Someone may reconsider a teaching they have repeated without examining the whole counsel of Scripture.
Someone may be encouraged to seek help.
And someone who has misused biblical authority may be confronted with the need to repent.
You don't need to reveal personal details or describe any trauma.
Or write, "Lord, teach Your Church to protect the wounded."
If you need prayer, you may say, "Please pray for me," without explaining why.
And if you have a testimony of healing, wisdom, or restoration that you freely wish to share, your words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
Let the comments become a place of biblical truth, compassion, and prayer, never a courtroom where survivors are pressured to prove their pain.
And if this ministry has helped you grow in your understanding of God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to creating Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotionals, and discipleship resources that encourage believers to move beyond surface-level faith.
We want these resources to continue reaching people who are hungry for biblical truth, including those who cannot afford to pay for them.
That work takes time, resources, consistency, and people willing to help sustain it.
Scripture calls believers to generosity that is willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
But if you are able and genuinely desire to partner with us, your monthly contribution can become one practical expression of generosity toward a ministry whose mission you believe in.
These products are simply another way to encourage faith, reflection, and meaningful conversations about Jesus. They are not the reason we preach the Gospel.
Christ is.
Praying for this ministry matters.
Speaking the truth in love matters.
Protecting the vulnerable matters.
Before you leave, I want you to remember the woman from the beginning of this article.
The one sitting beside her husband in church.
The one who heard him singing while she fought back tears.
The one who wondered whether God expected her to endure what frightened and wounded her.
Maybe she is someone you know.
Maybe she is someone you will meet.
Maybe she has been reading every word of this article with trembling hands.
Or maybe, for the first time, she is beginning to understand that the voice of the man who hurt her is not the voice of God.
If that woman is you, I pray you find safe people who will listen, qualified help that will protect you, and a clearer understanding of the Lord who created you with dignity.
Your life matters beyond your marriage.
Your safety matters beyond another person's reputation.
Your voice matters even when others would rather you remain silent.
And Jesus Christ is worthy of a Church that tells the truth, protects the vulnerable, confronts wrongdoing, and refuses to turn His holy Word into an instrument of cruelty.
Because the question was never whether a husband can claim authority over his wife.
The question is whether we will recognize that no human authority is permitted to make evil holy.
And if the Church truly belongs to Jesus, it must never ask a wounded woman to carry the shame of the person who harmed her.
The ring on her finger was supposed to remind her of a promise of love, not become the reason she was afraid to say no.
